content: Coronaviruses are a genus of animal viruses that belong to the family Coronaviridae. They are named for their crown-like surface projections, which resemble a corona under electron microscopy. The first coronavirus was isolated from chickens in 1937. In 1965, Tyrrell and Bynoe successfully propagated the first human coronavirus (HCoV) in vitro using cultures of human ciliated embryonal trachea. Currently, there are approximately 15 species within this family, which can infect a variety of hosts, including humans, cattle, pigs, rodents, cats, dogs, and birds. Some of these viruses are significant veterinary pathogens, particularly in chickens. Coronaviruses gained global attention during the severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) epidemic caused by SARS-CoV in 2002–2003. Another novel coronavirus, MERS-CoV, emerged in 2012, causing the Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS) epidemic. In 2019, a new coronavirus, 2019-nCoV (later named SARS-CoV-2), was identified as the cause of an outbreak of respiratory illness in Wuhan, China. Coronaviruses can be classified into three groups based on their genetic and structural characteristics. They can also be categorized by their genome and replication methods, as well as their ability to infect humans. These viruses are widespread globally and are responsible for 10–15% of common cold cases. Infections are strongly seasonal, with the highest incidence occurring in children during the winter months. Adult infections are less common. The exact number of coronavirus serotypes and the extent of antigenic variation remain unknown. Re-infections throughout life suggest the presence of multiple serotypes (at least four are known) and/or antigenic variation, which complicates the development of effective immunization strategies. The case fatality rates of coronaviruses vary depending on the strain. SARS had a case fatality rate of 9.6% with 8,098 confirmed cases. MERS had a significantly higher case fatality rate of 34.4% with 2,465 laboratory-confirmed cases. For 2019-nCoV, the case fatality rate among the first 99 patients hospitalized in Wuhan was reported to be 11%. Diagnosis is based on a combination of clinical and epidemiological criteria. Key diagnostic factors include close contact with infected individuals, travel to endemic areas, and the detection of viral RNA in the patient’s serum. Common symptoms include fever, cough, and shortness of breath. The incubation period varies depending on the specific virus, with the mean incubation period for 2019-nCoV estimated to be 5.2 days. Physical examination findings in coronavirus infections are non-specific but often include fever, flu-like symptoms, cough, and body aches. The general appearance of the patient depends on the stage of the illness. Chest X-rays in suspected cases may show findings similar to pneumonia. Electrocardiograms (ECGs) do not reveal specific abnormalities, but non-specific findings such as sinus tachycardia and diffuse T-wave inversion may be observed. Chest CT scans can reveal unilateral or bilateral pneumonia, ground-glass opacities, focal or multifocal opacities, consolidation, and septal thickening, with subpleural and lower lobe involvement being more common. Laboratory tests, including serology, molecular testing, and viral culture, can confirm coronavirus infections, but these are not routinely performed due to the typically mild nature of most infections and the limited availability of specialized laboratories. Other diagnostic tools, such as electron microscopy, PCR-based assays, and serological studies, are primarily used in research settings. There is no specific treatment for coronavirus infections. Management is supportive, focusing on alleviating symptoms and providing care for complications such as respiratory distress, which may require mechanical ventilation and intensive care. Most individuals with coronavirus infections recover without specific medical intervention. However, the prognosis depends on the type of virus involved, the severity of the disease, and the patient’s age, immune status, and presence of comorbid conditions. Young children, the elderly, immunocompromised individuals, and those with underlying health conditions are at higher risk for severe outcomes.
